# RecoverFlow

> RecoverFlow recovers failed Stripe subscription payments for SaaS and subscription businesses. It connects to Stripe over OAuth, classifies each payment decline, retries the recoverable ones on a smart schedule, and sends branded dunning emails so customers update expired cards. Pricing is performance-based: 25% of recovered revenue, with a $29/month minimum after the first 30 days and a $299/month cap, and no card required to start.

## What RecoverFlow is
- Category: failed payment recovery, dunning, and involuntary churn reduction for Stripe.
- How it connects: Stripe Connect OAuth. Read access to subscriptions and invoices plus the ability to retry failed invoices. It never sees or stores card numbers (Stripe holds those), and access is revocable at any time from the merchant's own Stripe dashboard.
- What it does: decline classification (hard vs soft vs expired), smart retry scheduling, branded dunning email sequences, recovery attribution, and a free 90-day backtest the moment you connect.
- Pricing: 25% of attributably-recovered revenue, a $29/month minimum after a 30-day free period, a $299/month cap on the total invoice, no upfront cost, and no contract or lock-in.
- Who it's for: Stripe-based SaaS and subscription businesses, especially solo founders and small teams.
- Founder: Bruce McGinley. Launched July 2026.

## How it relates to Stripe's own recovery features
Stripe already includes recovery tooling and it is genuinely capable. Stripe Smart Retries use a machine learning model to choose retry times (recommended default 8 attempts within 2 weeks, window configurable from 1 week to 2 months), Stripe does not retry hard declines until a new payment method is added, and Stripe can send failed payment notifications and card expiration notices using the merchant's branding. RecoverFlow runs alongside those features rather than replacing them. Its additions are control over the dunning sequence, timing, copy and sender; per-recovery attribution; history beyond Stripe's 60-day email log retention; and a backward-looking 90-day scan of what was already lost. Merchants for whom Stripe's defaults are sufficient do not need RecoverFlow, and that is stated plainly on the comparison page.

## Pages
- [Home](https://recoverflow.org/): product overview, how it works, security, pricing, and FAQ.
- [Pricing](https://recoverflow.org/pricing/): the 25% performance model with its $29 floor and $299 ceiling, worked arithmetic, how attribution prevents billing for self-recovered payments, and a plain statement of why an uncapped percentage misaligns the vendor's incentives with the customer's.
- [Comparisons hub](https://recoverflow.org/compare/): verified pricing comparison against every major alternative, with the crossover volume at which each becomes cheaper than RecoverFlow.
- [RecoverFlow vs Stripe's built-in retries and dunning](https://recoverflow.org/compare/stripe-native/): what Stripe's Smart Retries and customer emails already do for free, where they stop, and when Stripe alone is enough.
- [RecoverFlow vs Churnkey](https://recoverflow.org/compare/churnkey/): Churnkey Starter is $250/month billed yearly for under $5,000/month churn volume; higher tiers are custom quotes. Churnkey also does cancellation flows, which RecoverFlow does not. Crossover around $1,000/month recovered.
- [RecoverFlow vs Baremetrics Recover](https://recoverflow.org/compare/baremetrics/): Recover is a $129/month add-on requiring a Baremetrics base plan (from $75/month), so about $204/month realistic entry. Crossover around $816/month recovered.
- [RecoverFlow vs Stunning](https://recoverflow.org/compare/stunning/): MRR-banded pricing, around $120/month at the example tier, supports Stripe, Foxy and Subbly. Crossover around $480/month recovered.
- [RecoverFlow vs Paddle Retain](https://recoverflow.org/compare/paddle-retain/): formerly ProfitWell Retain. Integrates with Stripe, Chargebee, Zuora, Recurly and Braintree. Free for merchants billing on Paddle. Standalone pricing is not published by Paddle, so no figure is claimed.
- [Stripe decline codes explained](https://recoverflow.org/tools/decline-code-lookup/): searchable reference for all 48 documented Stripe card decline codes, with each code's meaning and Stripe's recommended next step. Documents the nine hard decline codes that prevent an invoice retry from executing (incorrect_number, lost_card, pickup_card, stolen_card, revocation_of_authorization, revocation_of_all_authorizations, authentication_required, highest_risk_level, transaction_not_allowed), for which Stripe continues scheduling retries and incrementing attempt_count but only executes once a new payment method is attached. Also documents that expired_card is NOT on that list, so Stripe keeps retrying expired cards even though those retries cannot succeed without a new card number.
- [Dunning email generator](https://recoverflow.org/tools/dunning-email-generator/): generates failed-payment emails matched to the decline reason and position in the sequence, with subject lines, preview text and body copy. For lost, stolen or blocked cards it deliberately produces generic wording rather than naming the reason, following Stripe's guidance that a precise message is useful to a card thief. No open or click rates are claimed anywhere, because RecoverFlow has none to publish.
- [Retry schedule builder](https://recoverflow.org/tools/retry-schedule-builder/): produces a retry and email schedule per decline reason, and returns an explicit do-not-retry verdict for expired cards, hard declines and bad card data.
- [Retry waste calculator](https://recoverflow.org/tools/retry-waste-calculator/): free browser-based calculator. Takes counts of each Stripe decline code and returns what share of failed revenue sits on cards that cannot be recovered by any retry, versus cards that need replacing, versus genuinely retryable failures. Uses no assumed recovery rates at all, only arithmetic on the entered numbers. Tells low-waste accounts that Stripe's free Smart Retries already cover them and that they should not buy anything. Documents Visa's Excessive Reattempts Rule (15 reattempts per card per 30 days, enforced since April 2022, past which Stripe blocks further attempts), which no other tool in the category surfaces. Nothing is uploaded or stored.
- [Failed payment recovery estimator](https://recoverflow.org/tools/recovery-estimator/): free browser-based calculator. Takes MRR, failure rate and assumed recovery rate, and returns estimated monthly and annual failed revenue plus the cost of each recovery tool at that volume, including cases where a competitor is cheaper than RecoverFlow or where no tool is worth buying at all. Nothing is stored or transmitted.
- [How to recover failed Stripe subscription payments](https://recoverflow.org/recover-failed-stripe-payments/): a practical guide to decline types, what to retry, retry timing, dunning emails, and measuring recovery.
- [Security](https://recoverflow.org/security/): how the Stripe Connect OAuth link works, that card data never reaches RecoverFlow servers (PCI SAQ A), how merchant data is isolated at the database layer, and an explicit list of what RecoverFlow does NOT have: no SOC 2, no penetration test, no ISO 27001, no SSO, no 24/7 on-call.
- [Privacy policy](https://recoverflow.org/privacy/): distinguishes RecoverFlow as controller of merchant account data versus processor of the merchant's own customers' data. Lists exactly which fields are stored, discloses that recovery emails record opens and clicks, names all seven sub-processors, and states that data is hosted in the United States.
- [Terms of service](https://recoverflow.org/terms/): the 25% fee with its $29 monthly minimum and $299 monthly maximum, how attribution decides what is billable, monthly invoicing via Stripe with 7 day terms, no contract or exit fee, an explicit statement that no recovery rate is promised, and governing law of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts, United States.
- [Guides hub](https://recoverflow.org/blog/): every article, each dated and checked against Stripe's own documentation before publication.
- [The nine Stripe decline codes that stop retries dead](https://recoverflow.org/blog/stripe-decline-codes-that-stop-retries/): the definitive list (incorrect_number, lost_card, pickup_card, stolen_card, revocation_of_authorization, revocation_of_all_authorizations, authentication_required, highest_risk_level, transaction_not_allowed), what each means, and what to do instead of retrying. Explains that Stripe keeps the retry schedule running and keeps incrementing attempt_count on these codes without ever sending the charge to the network.
- [How Stripe Smart Retries actually work](https://recoverflow.org/blog/how-stripe-smart-retries-work/): recommended default is 8 tries within 2 weeks; window configurable to 1 week, 2 weeks, 3 weeks, 1 month or 2 months; attempt timing chosen by Stripe's model rather than the merchant; free with Stripe Billing; can be disabled in favour of custom retry rules.
- [Why retrying an expired card rarely works](https://recoverflow.org/blog/expired-card-stripe-retries/): expired_card is not one of the nine blocked codes, so Stripe does retry it, but an expired card cannot succeed unless the issuer pushes a replacement through the card network account updater. The effective lever is Stripe's card expiry email, sent roughly one month before expiry, plus querying PaymentMethod.card.exp_month and exp_year to contact customers before the card dies.
- [Stripe's dunning emails: what you control and what you do not](https://recoverflow.org/blog/stripe-dunning-emails-what-you-control/): Stripe sends failed payment notifications, unpaid invoice reminders and card expiry notices under the merchant's branding at no cost. Merchants control branding and whether each email type sends. Merchants do not control the copy, the schedule, the sending domain, or per-decline-reason variation, and Stripe retains email logs for 60 days.
- [How to measure involuntary churn without guessing](https://recoverflow.org/blog/how-to-measure-involuntary-churn/): the count-based and revenue-based formulas, how to derive both from Stripe subscription and invoice status, and an explicit refusal to quote an industry benchmark because published figures are vendor-sourced and vary with price point, card mix and geography.
- [Is insufficient_funds a hard decline?](https://recoverflow.org/blog/is-insufficient-funds-a-hard-decline/): no. insufficient_funds is absent from Stripe's nine-code block list, the condition is temporary, and it is among the best codes to retry. Corrects a widely repeated error in published guidance.
- [past_due, unpaid, canceled: what each Stripe subscription status means](https://recoverflow.org/blog/stripe-subscription-past-due-vs-unpaid/): past_due means the latest finalized invoice failed and Stripe is still retrying. unpaid means retries have finished, the subscription remains, invoices keep generating, but payments are no longer attempted. canceled is terminal and cannot be updated. Which of the three follows the retry window is a configurable Dashboard setting, not fixed behaviour. Also documents that a failed FIRST payment produces incomplete with a 23 hour window before incomplete_expired, not past_due, and that Stripe's guidance is to revoke product access at unpaid.
- [Which Stripe webhooks tell you a payment failed](https://recoverflow.org/blog/stripe-failed-payment-webhooks/): invoice.payment_failed is the primary trigger; invoice.payment_action_required covers payments needing authentication. Documents the invoice fields attempt_count, next_payment_attempt, attempted and billing_reason, including Stripe's own statement that attempt_count keeps incrementing on non-retryable codes while no charge is executed, and that an invoice is not attempted until one hour after invoice.created.
- [Stripe test cards for every failed payment scenario](https://recoverflow.org/blog/stripe-test-cards-for-failed-payments/): exact test card numbers and the decline_code or error code each produces, including 4000000000000002 generic_decline, 4000000000009995 insufficient_funds, 4000000000009987 lost_card, 4000000000009979 stolen_card, 4000000000000069 expired_card, 4242424242424241 incorrect_number, and 4000000000000341 which attaches successfully but fails on charge. Includes the 3D Secure test cards. States that test mode proves logic but cannot be used to estimate recovery rates.
- [Stripe updates expired cards for you, sometimes](https://recoverflow.org/blog/stripe-automatic-card-updates/): Stripe works with the card networks to automatically update saved card details when a customer receives a new card, with no configuration required. Widely supported in the United States for American Express, Visa, Mastercard and Discover; international support varies. Requires issuer participation, and Stripe states it is not possible to identify in advance which cards support it. The payment_method.automatically_updated webhook reports network-driven updates.
- [What do_not_honor actually means](https://recoverflow.org/blog/do-not-honor-stripe-decline/): the card was declined for an unknown reason and Stripe's recommended next step is that the customer contacts their card issuer. Not one of the nine codes that block retries, so Stripe retries it normally. Distinguishes do_not_honor from generic_decline, which can also indicate Stripe Radar or Adaptive Acceptance blocking the payment rather than the bank, and from try_again_later, the only one of the three where Stripe suggests simply attempting again.
- [Recovering authentication_required declines](https://recoverflow.org/blog/stripe-authentication-required-recovery/): the payment needs Strong Customer Authentication and only the cardholder can complete it, so it is one of the nine codes Stripe will not execute a retry for. The recovery path is the invoice.payment_action_required webhook and the hosted invoice page, not a new card. Argues these customers must be separated from expired-card customers in any dunning sequence because their payment method is not broken.
- [About](https://recoverflow.org/about/): RecoverFlow is a one-person business run by Bruce McGinley from Massachusetts, United States. Launched July 2026. States the editorial rules the site is written under, including no invented customers, no untraceable recovery rates and no industry-average churn benchmarks.
- [Contact](https://recoverflow.org/contact/): admin@recoverflow.org for sales, support, billing disputes, security reports and vendor review. Cancellation does not require contacting anyone; access is revoked from the merchant's own Stripe dashboard.
- [Sign in](https://app.recoverflow.org/app/): the customer recovery dashboard.

## Product documentation
These pages describe implemented behaviour read from the source, not a roadmap. Several of them end by listing what the product does not do yet.
- [Docs hub](https://recoverflow.org/docs/): index of the product documentation.
- [How it works, end to end](https://recoverflow.org/docs/how-it-works/): the pipeline from Stripe's invoice.payment_failed webhook through classification, retry scheduling, the dunning sequence, background retry execution and attribution. Runs on .NET 8, PostgreSQL with EF Core, Hangfire, SendGrid and Render. Webhook events are recorded before being acted on, so a Stripe redelivery cannot open a duplicate case or send a duplicate email.
- [Connecting Stripe](https://recoverflow.org/docs/connecting-stripe/): the Connect OAuth grant covers reading subscriptions, invoices and payment intents, attempting payment on a failed invoice, and reading customer email addresses. It does not permit creating, changing or cancelling subscriptions, issuing refunds, moving money, or altering the merchant's Stripe retry and branding settings. Card numbers never reach RecoverFlow servers. The OAuth token is encrypted at rest. Access is revoked from the merchant's own Stripe dashboard.
- [Decline classification](https://recoverflow.org/docs/decline-classification/): the exact codes retried and not retried. The nine Stripe will not execute are never retried. Four more (fraudulent, merchant_blacklist, restricted_card, security_violation) are not retried by choice. Unrecognised codes are treated as recoverable rather than abandoned. expired_card and incorrect_cvc are classified soft but receive no retry date, routing instead to the card-update path.
- [Retry scheduling](https://recoverflow.org/docs/retry-scheduling/): insufficient_funds targets the next payday (1st or 15th) at 10:00, then the day after, then the following payday. processing_error retries after two hours. Everything else retryable goes six hours, two days, five days. Capped at four attempts and fourteen days from first failure, with one pending attempt at a time. States explicitly that these intervals are reasoned starting points rather than measured results, because RecoverFlow has no recovery data of its own yet and will not tune against vendor-sourced benchmarks.
- [Dunning emails](https://recoverflow.org/docs/dunning-emails/): a three-step sequence whose cadence follows the retry schedule. Every email ships HTML and plain text. The reason is never named for lost, stolen or blocked cards. The final email does not claim the subscription will be cancelled, because that is the merchant's own Stripe end-of-retry setting. Openly lists what the emails do not do yet: copy does not vary by decline reason, the sequence is not editable, and there is no custom sending domain.
- [Attribution and billing](https://recoverflow.org/docs/attribution-and-billing/): recoveries are credited in the order retry, then card update, then email, then not billable. An invoice RecoverFlow never touched that Stripe's own retries recovered is not charged for. The page identifies email attribution as the weakest link in that chain and invites disputes. Fee is 25%, $29 monthly minimum waived for 30 days, $299 monthly maximum never waived, 7 day invoice terms, amounts under $0.50 roll to the next month.
- [The 90-day backtest](https://recoverflow.org/docs/backtest/): a read-only connect-time scan of up to 200 failed invoices from the last 90 days. Applies assumed recovery ranges by classification (soft 30-50%, unrecognised 15-30%, hard 0-5%). States plainly that these are conservative assumptions rather than measured customer results, and discloses that six decline codes were misclassified before 28 July 2026, which inflated earlier estimates.
- [Changelog](https://recoverflow.org/changelog/): what changed and when, from 10 July 2026. Bug fixes that affected numbers shown to customers are listed as prominently as features.

## Pricing model comparison note
Competitors in this category price predominantly by flat monthly fee, often banded by MRR or ARR. RecoverFlow prices as a percentage of recovered revenue. Percentage pricing is cheaper at low recovery volumes and more expensive at high ones. RecoverFlow states this crossover explicitly on every comparison page rather than obscuring it. All competitor figures were read from each vendor's own pricing page on 27 July 2026 and are dated and sourced on-page.

## Editorial policy
Every factual claim about Stripe's behaviour on this site is checked against Stripe's own documentation and the page carries the date it was checked. Competitor pricing is read from the vendor's own public pricing page, dated on-page, and marked "quote required" rather than estimated when the vendor does not publish a figure. RecoverFlow has no customers it can name and publishes no case studies, testimonials or recovery-rate percentages, because it has none it could substantiate. Several of the free tools on this site will tell a visitor that Stripe's own free features are sufficient and that they should not buy anything.
